utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, The Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Before we continue to hear the evidence of the witness, there's one issue I'd like to raise immediately, and that deals with the redacted witness statement of Miroslav Homa [phoen]. On the 18th of November, that was yesterday, the Chamber admitted the redacted witness statement of witness Miroslav Homa into evidence, pending the filing of an attestation and declaration in compliance with the requirements of Rule 92 bis (B) of the Rules. The Chamber notes that only the witness's unredacted statement has been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter number 1D01689. The Chamber hereby instructs the Defence to upload or release the redacted witness statement as attached to the Defence motion. The Chamber also already instructs the Registry to assign the redacted numbers to the exhibit number of the witness statement. And could that be done as quickly as possible. Then could the witness be escorted in the courtroom. Mr. Weber, unless -- is there any urgent matter you have?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I was just going to keep the process going of doing some housekeeping as the witness is coming in, if that is acceptable to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time, the Prosecution has uploaded the handwritten notes on the list from the witness under 65 ter 33515. We have submitted it for translation. If we could please have the 65 ter marked for identification at this time with an exhibit number, it would be appreciated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 65 ter 33515 would receive number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P7674, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification. I take it there that may be some further discussion once it has been translated what the probative value of that document would be, so whether it meets all requirements for admission.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It is, and if there's any --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In those discussions, if there's any other things that are needed to make it clear, we will also discuss that with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Good morning, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am afraid that we will not conclude your testimony today, which we regret. We would have very much liked to accommodate you. That's one. Second, we have no possibility for extended sessions and neither a session tomorrow. That's -- if we can, we usually try to accommodate, but we're also afraid that it would not assist sufficiently to conclude your this week. I don't know what problems this causes to you. If there are urgent problems, which are difficult to overcome, then, of course, we would have to briefly discuss it. But, as matters stand now, we do not expect you to conclude your testimony before the weekend. Mr. Weber will now continue his cross-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were you able to locate that 1994 document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps from the deputy commander that we discussed yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I looked and I found several documents, but this specific one that I spoke about; it's paragraph 497 of the report in the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much for checking that. I'm going to continue and I may come back to that in the next session. In the introduction and parts 1 through 3 of your report, you do not refer to many primary sources, so I'm not going to spend much more time talking to you about the topics related to these sections; however, I do still have a couple of things to go through related to them and the couple primary sources that you do refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 1D05358, page 72 in the B/C/S and page 73 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 3.1 of your report, you discuss a bunch of facts related to events in Bosanski Brod, starting from 3 March 1992 and thereafter. You talk about attacks, the geography, military units, excavations of bodies and so on. Now, in the footnote, footnote 159, the only source you cite in this paragraph is Branko Lukic's opening statement in the Stakic case on 18 November 1992. In your view, is an opening statement an authoritative source for topics you discuss in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as of this paragraph is concerned, I checked this in a number of reports and documents relating to the war-time-period discussed, i.e., the analysis, newspaper articles. There were several sources that refer to this period and this particular area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to go back to my original question. So, first, is an opening statement an authoritative source for what you cite in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I'm concerned, yes; but, like I said, I did consult other sources too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now this has come up a couple of times during the course of your examination and it relates to an issue of transparency, and you have often said, Ah, I have consulted many sources, documents, newspapers, I believe you just said just now, but the fact is you didn't put these in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that I would take one source that I believed relevant out of a number of sources to indicate what the material in my report is based on. As far as this particular point, I saw some documents, notes regarding crimes that occurred in that area. I saw at least four or five video recordings of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you didn't put any of those video recordings in this paragraph, right, you didn't cite to any of them?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not. Because, like I said, I don't believe that it's necessary to refer to each and every source in the paragraphs that I put in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: How about this? I just wonder about this in terms of your methodology: Did you even check the Stakic judgement to see what happened -- if what happened in Bosanski Brod was even relevant to the facts in those proceedings or even to see whether or not there are any documentary materials showing that widespread crimes were committed against non-Serbs in the vicinity of Prijedor or in the Omarska, Keraterm and Trnopolje camps? Did you do any of that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did watch the footage, not in the Stakic case, but I did view the video material that showed the crimes that occurred at that time in that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You didn't cite that stuff in your report, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These events were not described here and they were not the topic of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You didn't think they were relevant to this case?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that the sources were not relevant. It's just that I did not describe those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You agree that one would need to actually look at 1 KK, 1st Krajina Corps, orders and reports from 1992 in order to even attempt an analysis of the VRS actions throughout many of the municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina during this time; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. If I were to review each locality and each municipality, each region in Bosnia-Herzegovina then I would need five years in order to write my expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, in your report, you do not reference a single document from the 1st Krajina Corps. I put it to you that you have not done a credible analysis related to the VRS's actions or General Mladic's role throughout the entire zone of responsibility in the municipalities that are covered by the 1st Krajina Corps; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not deal overly with the 1st Krajina Corps, but the final operations of the Army of the Republic of Croatia and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. In Republika Srpska, I did not focus on that in my report. Mainly, I focussed on Sarajevo and the protected areas of Srebrenica and Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. In your report, specifically paragraphs 2. -- excuse me, I'll start again. 2.75, 3.67, 3.70, 5.72, and 5.82 to 5.84, you do refer to VRS Main Staff Directives 7, 7.1, and 8. There are not any references to Main Staff Directives 1 through 6 and Directive 9 in your report. I put it to you that do you not credibly discuss the role of the VRS Main Staff or General Mladic in his commanding role throughout much of the war without analysing directives such as the ones I just mentioned in conjunction with other military documents that show their implementation; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't agree. Directive 4 and Directive 7.1 are key ones relating to those -- these two areas that I mentioned earlier, where combat was happening during the civil war in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your analysis of that is limited to your consideration of what happened in the enclaves of Srebrenica and Zepa; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sarajevo, Srebrenica and Zepa, because these are the main elements of the indictment. So when I was deciding on the contents of my report, that's how I structured the contents, and you can see that from the general structure of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So in Directive 4, with respect to Sarajevo, you consider that General Mladic assigns tasks to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps including the fact that he ordered the SRK's main forces to keep Sarajevo and Igman under full blockade and, in accordance with the developments, tighten the circle and cut off and isolate parts of the city and surrounding settlements. You considered that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please show me this directive? That section that you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have P1968, page 11 in the B/C/S and page 5 of the translation. And focussing on section (e) of this directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, my question is very simple: Did you consider this when you discuss events in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did consider it, in detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Why didn't you include discussion of it in your Sarajevo section of your report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see anything here that would require to be part of the discussion. When I see it here, I can see that terms are being used that you mentioned in your question and that you cited.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. So General Mladic's directives weren't important for you, for you to cite.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection. Misstates the evidence of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes. That's not for the witness, so if you would please -- But you considered apparently this part of the directive, not to contain relevant information so as to deal with it in your report, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I did consider the directive, but in the way that I actually considered the relevant -- the elements and the assignments issued to the corps, the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. But what I'm saying is that item (e) does not contain the terms that you were used in the question that was put to me. What it says here is to "keep" Sarajevo, not what was said earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's have a look at the question. Let me just ... one second, please. What was read in the question to you is, please compare it carefully with what's on your screen. Whether you considered that General Mladic's assigns tasks to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, including the fact that he ordered the SRK's main forces to keep Sarajevo and Igman under full blockade and in accordance with the developments, tighten the circle and cut off and isolate parts of the city and surrounding settlements. That's what was read to you. And is what you think is not to be found in paragraph (e) on this page?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you find it there, but it's not verbatim and the terms are not identical. It says here at the very beginning "to keep in the blockade."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think Mr. Weber quoted, if not fully verbatim then approximately verbatim what is read. There may be a translation issue, I do not know. But perhaps -- I don't know how it was translated in B/C/S. But what Mr. Weber put to you is whether you considered, whether you -- I think the gist of it was whether you considered it relevant to refer to what is written in paragraph (e) of this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did consider it relevant, and I put forward my position that this was a military blockade, a blockade of the city, and I distinguished between an encircled or besieged town, and these terms helped me -- these terms from the orders helped me to formulate these positions on top of general theoretical concepts. And I believe that keeping a part of Sarajevo under blockade was a legitimate military act.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It was not part of the question, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 41351, you were asked about a portion of Sir Richard Dannatt's testimony about the 2nd Military District. The question was: "What can you say to about this is it fair or accurate to -- is that true VRS, in essence, was the 2nd Military District or that the Main Staff of the VRS equated to the command of that district?" Your answer was: "Quite frankly, there are no facts to support this kind of assertion and this kind of position cannot be based on the projection of personnel or material or the establishment of the Military District when compared to the Army of Republika Srpska." Now, in part 2 of your report, in paragraph 2.48, you state that "the existing elements of the commands of the 2nd VO were the core around which the initial elements of the GS" - which I take it you're referring to the Main Staff - "were formed." Your own report contradicts the answer you gave in court; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think if counsel is going to use the report I think the procedure in this courtroom has been to show the report in both languages so that we all can follow. I don't know why we're departing from that procedure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- understanding this not as a question as why it is done wrongly but an invitation for you to do that, Mr. Weber, I think you'd certainly follow that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I do think the witness has it in front of him. If he needs to refer to it, I will try to get the page numbers quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It is page 62 in hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And 62 in e-court as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... 62 in e-court in the English and ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: B/C/S, it should be the previous page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And page 61 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said specifically, also in terms of structure, that it cannot be the same level of command, not if you compare the global organisation of the Military District and the Main Staff of the VRS, there is no overlap, neither in terms of function nor in any other sense. In terms of personnel, the functions and the duties formulated in the Military District do not coincide with those of the Main Staff. In the structure of the personnel, there is no similarity, let alone identicality. I said even then that a number of officers, not from the Military District but from various areas made up the core, the inner circle of the Main Staff which later grew. So there is no coincidence between those two commands, not even similarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you stand by your statement that the existing elements of the 2nd VO were the core around which the initial elements of the Main Staff were formed. You stand by that; right?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the quote be repeated with the exact reference to the text, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 2.48, you stand by your statement that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The very last sentence of 2.48.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, please read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The last sentence of paragraph 2.48, I'm quoting: "The existing elements of the command of the 2nd VO were the core around which the initial elements of the GS were formed."

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see what's in dispute here. When you say "elements" then one part --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the question is whether you stand by that, whether you still -- whether this is still --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I stand by that statement. I just want to clarify what it refers to, what it means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Weber was primarily interested to know whether you stand by it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: As support for your -- for this paragraph, you referred to the 23 January 1992 2nd Military District combat readiness report related to the year 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 05580, page 2 of the B/C/S and page 1 of the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is the 2nd Military District combat readiness report that you referred to; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 4 in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the bottom of the page, it indicates that the -- at the beginning of January 1992, referring to 10 January 1992, that the command of the 5th Military District was renamed the 2nd Military District and it came to comprise new units and a new zone of responsibility. The 2nd Military District was established on 10th of May -- or 10th of January, 1992; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 28 of the B/C/S and page 23 of the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the bottom of this page, the report indicates: "The changes in the organisation and establishment of the commands and units of the 2nd VO have improved and enhanced the manoeuvrability of units, contributed to more efficient command and control, the provisions -- the provision of combat support, and the organisation and possibilities for armed struggle." Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we have a more precise reference for the original, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Page 28 of the B/C/S. At the bottom of the page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you then read it again, Mr. Weber, slowly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, the part that I am referring to is the part that says: "The changes in organisation and establishment of the commands and units of the 2nd VO have improved and enhanced the manoeuvrability of units, contributed to more efficient command and control, the provision of combat support, organisation and possibilities for armed struggle." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the conclusion of this report. Concerning certain elements, you can agree that, yes, there were positive effects, but not the whole conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And you realise that many of the -- that the corps and its -- many of the subordinate units of the 2nd Military District did then become part of the Army of Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only part of their forces -- and I mean some of the equipment, infrastructure, logistics. Just like the case was with the deployment of these units in the entire territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I said that at the beginning. Depending on which area these units with their logistics were, later they became part of the national army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness also explain to us. He said he partly shared the conclusions but not all, not the whole conclusion. In what respect do you not agree with the conclusion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The part which talks about the entire Military District, whereas only some of their assets were in the territory of Republika Srpska. And it's a fact that only a part of the equipment which was not pulled back to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia were used in Republika Srpska. Parts of the equipment that were in areas that were later taken by Croatian and Muslim forces were taken, mostly successfully, by the Croatian and Muslim forces, whereas, it says here that the entire Military District became the basis for establishing the Army of Republika Srpska, which is not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do you read that exactly, the entire, in this portion that was read to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, when it says "changes in the commands and units of the 2nd Military District have contributed to," it doesn't say parts of commands and units. It says "the commands and units," which means, implicitly, the entire Military District.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And then you say not all of that was in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Does it say anywhere that this only applies for what happened in Bosnia-Herzegovina? Because I didn't read that either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This talks primarily about the report relating to the Army of Republika Srpska. So what is meant are assets and personnel that were in the Serbian territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and became part of the future army, and it doesn't refer to the part of the equipment and personnel that were withdrawn to the territory of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Prosecution tenders the document into evidence, 65 ter 05880 [sic].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I think it's 05580?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives exhibit number P7675, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Let's have a look at -- what's the entire document is, how many pages --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it is a combat readiness assessment so it is a little bit larger of a document. There are many attachments to it. I think it is important in light of all the evidence that the Chamber does have in front of it relating to the units, and many of the attachments refer to the specific units and their composition that we actually need the full document in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the full document would mean how many pages?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Kindly slow down for the sake of the interpreters, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In B/C/S, it is 104, much of which is the attachments.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, select relevant portions that you used with this witness and if there's any need just for two or three quotes, the Chamber is not going to accept 104 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, I understand the Chamber's concern. I am asking exceptionally that it be allowed at least to have the full text of the report and then some limited attachments which would substantially reduce the overall size of the material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: To what?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just checking the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. At this moment, I think the -- what is on my screen as this report is seven pages, so I'm a bit ... no, I'm sorry, I'm looking at the wrong one. That's the -- was the previous one. Make a selection, Mr. Weber. If you think we do not need all the annexes then start striking the annexes but we are not, on the basis of the evidence given by this witness, at this moment we're not going to admit 104 pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I will, of course, be guided by the Chamber. The Prosecution's concern is just that the witness has articulated opinions so and this is a document he references in his report. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you, first of all, would slow down. I think you've taken the witnesses to some portions which apparently contradict, in the Prosecution's view, what he stated in his report and we should look at that. But we are not going then to analyse the whole of the report against 104 pages contained in this report. So at this moment, the number just assigned by Madam Registrar is reserved for an excerpt which we will still see to be uploaded in e-court. The Defence has an opportunity to add whatever it thinks needs for contextualisation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33437.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 4 July 1992 decision to organise and establish the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The fact is, is that the ABiH was formally established on this date, on 4 July, and existed before and out of the formations that were the Territorial Defence units before that; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It developed from the paramilitary units of the Patriotic League, Green Berets and the Territorial Defence taken together.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 33437 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33437 receives exhibit number P7676.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33350 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 12 May 1992 order from the 17th Corps command. Under item 2, the order instructs: "Conduct a mobilisation of the combat-fit Serbian population ..." Around the time of the VRS being established, the VRS was interested in mobilising the Serb population; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I see the signature, please. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree with the document. As for your assertion, the Yugoslav People's Army, at that time - that means a month into the civil war - left -- in fact, Croatian personnel and officers, most of them, left the Yugoslav People's Army. The JNA started withdrawing, and the part of the equipment that was planned to be transported to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia could not be pulled out without the men, without the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You've explained a lot of this in your report. I would encourage you to just so we could move along, if you could stay to the topic. I was asking about mobilisation. I think you've answered the question even in your explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please tender 65 ter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I haven't heard an answer to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was the VRS interested in mobilising, for whatever reasons, the Serb population around the time when the VRS was established?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In its -- in their own units. That was already the beginning, the day of the establishment of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I tender 65 ter 33350 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, if you do it a bit slower then the chance that numbers are not recorded well; although they were now. That risk is diminished. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33350 receives exhibit number P7677, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 1D05358, page 113 of the B/C/S and page 115 of the English version. If we could focus, please, on paragraph 4.33.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4.33 of your report, it starts: "On 22 April 1992, Muslim armed units and the HVO launched an all-out attack on Ilidza despite the previously reached agreement on the Cessation of Hostilities." The paragraph appears to discuss the attack up until the last sentence. This paragraph contains what purports to be factual descriptions of an attack on 22 April; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The elements, the framework of that event, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You do not reference any sources in this paragraph to support these facts, do you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's possible that there is no reference given, but I want to remind you that I looked at the report and footage of combat action from that day in the area of Ilidza. I saw video recordings. And even two video reports by British journalists who happened to be in Ilidza on that day. Their reports were the basis for my description in general terms of this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I have no idea what reports you're talking about. But could you not locate a single military document that discusses the events of 22 April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I found them and I looked at them, including those two video reports. I didn't consider it necessary to go into detail. My intention was, rather, to show how ten days after signing a truce, Muslim forces and part of the Croatian forces launched offensive action against the purely Serb municipality of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I put it on the record that the Prosecution has tendered into evidence reports of Ilidza and what was going on through some British journalists that they brought as witnesses, one that I remember, in particular.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It raises for me the question whether what the witness refers to - and we do not know what exactly he refers to - whether that is in evidence, yes or no. And that's, I think, one of the functions of footnotes that it enables those who are reading a document to check, to verify whether having access to those sources, if we have, and that's the first question, whether that supports the conclusions as drawn. I'm -- could you tell us a bit more in detail what videos you looked at so we could start, at least, guessing whether that is material which is available to this Chamber, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two video recordings and reports by British journalists who happened to be in that area. And I didn't view them yesterday to be able to describe all the details and tell you which journalists, for which TV station. If there is anything in this paragraph that is questionable or in dispute, you could point it to me and then I could explain. Just looking at it now, I cannot remember, but I know what I watched. I watched a huge number of recordings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you said two. Were there more than two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Two by British reporters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, there may be something in dispute. There may not be something in dispute; but we're unable to even think about that if we don't have access to the sources you say you've used and which are not specified. Could the parties try to see, Mr. Ivetic, you apparently have some memory about videos from that date so that, at least, we could start guessing whether we have material which may be the same material as the witness relied on. Apart from the two British videos, do you have any other of the -- you said you looked at -- you said even, I think, a huge number, but ... huge number. Could you give us a bit more information about had huge amount of video material you verified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, next time I can bring precise references, both concerning these two British reports and the other sources on which this paragraph relies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you mean by "next time" one of the coming days or ... because I don't expect you to come back in this courtroom again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A moment ago, it was said the trial will continue. If it does, then my next appearance here I will bring them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that there may be some misunderstanding. This trial will continue by hearing your evidence today, Monday, and -- or at least -- one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least we'll continue, although interrupted by some other evidence early next week. So if you have that material available early next week and that would be appreciated, if you have any information just write it down what it is, give it to VWS and VWS will give it to the parties and to the Bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what I meant, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But please include in your list of documents also the military reports you were referring to earlier today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, it means all the underlying materials from paragraph 4.33 you hinted at.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 08680.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic [sic], I'm also looking at the clock. I don't know how much time you would need with that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will try to go through very quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, by speaking very quickly, you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Hopefully --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If it is one or two minutes, okay. If it's more, we'll take the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's okay, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Process of elimination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic will be happy we're thinking of him even if he's not present in the courtroom. My apologies to both of you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This the JNA 2nd Military District report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so, I said if you can do it in one or two minutes, fine. Otherwise, we'll take the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to try to with a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the 2nd Military District report for 22 April 1992. Did you review this document?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did review it. I looked at the main points that I thought were relevant to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions. In the section on the 4th Corps, there's reference to the very complex situation that threatens to escalate into large-scale interethnic clashes and then it states: "The overall situation in Sarajevo is creating even [sic] greater uncertainty and concern among the population. At about 1900 hours, heavy weapons again opened fired [sic] on Sarajevo old town." You did not include the fact that the Sarajevo old town was fired upon on this date in your discussion of 22 April 1992, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Conflicts had already broken out between JNA units and paramilitary Muslim formations. These conflicts were going on for already a month. As for this here specifically, where was this projectile fired from and from which unit? That you don't see anywhere here. At that time there was no cease-fire or peace. On the 6th of April, the civil war had already started; and on the 12th of April, the Presidency of the BiH issued a decision or a directive, which we discussed, regarding the attitude or the position towards units of the JNA as enemy forces. The same situation was the same here, on the 22nd of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 08680 receives exhibit number P7678, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Then we'll take the break now. Witness, we'd like to see you back in 20 minutes. We'll take a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While the witness is not in yet, Mr. Weber, I would like to briefly address the following. On the 16th of November of this year, during the testimony of this same witness, Mr. Mitar Kovac, D1357, an excerpt from the manual on the Law on Armed Conflict was marked for identification pending agreement between the parties as to the excerpt to be tendered. That's found at 41379 to -380 and 41472 to -473. On the 18 November the Defence advised via e-mail that the parties agreed on the excerpts to be tendered into evidence and uploaded into e-court as document bearing Rule 65 ter number 1D01255a. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace D1357 with a new excerpt and admits D1357 into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Weber -- please do not proceed because Judge Fluegge has one or more questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, before the break I said to you that, please, include in your list of documents also the military reports you were referring to earlier today. And then you said: I don't understand. And therefore, I would like to help you to understand what I'm talking about. On page 20 were asked by Mr. Weber: "But could you not locate a single military document that discusses the events of 22 April 1992?" Your answer was: "Yes, I found them, and I looked at them." And then you continued: "Including those two video reports." These military documents you said you found them and looked at them should be included in the last you promised us, to give us, next week. Do you understand now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I have a part of these document with me on my laptop, and I'm not sure if I have one or several reports, but I do have these two video reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The second item I want to raise you -- and that can be found on page 7, there you said to a question of Mr. Weber: "Sarajevo, Srebrenica and Zepa, because these are the main elements of the indictment." I would kindly ask you to help me to find reference to Zepa in the indictment. Can you help me in that respect?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're talking about protected areas so, of course, because of the operation itself, the context of the area, I also spoke about Zepa. When you speak about Srebrenica and everything that happened in relation to Srebrenica, then it was normal also for me to look at that area around Zepa as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But you said something else. You said: These are the main elements of the indictment. Zepa as a main element of the indictment. Or was it just a slip of the tongue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's being presented differently, out of the context. When you talk about Krivaja 95 operation then both protected areas are referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you not answering my question or understanding it. Or at least you are not answering it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, at the outset of today, I asked you for a reference to where I could find a document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and I -- the transcript, and I believe I heard you to say paragraph 497. Did I understand -- is that correct, that that's the paragraph where I would find the document from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noted a number of paragraphs here but the one that refers to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps is paragraph 169, footnote 433.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, let me repeat that: --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat these numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, could you please repeat the numbers you just provided.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paragraph 4.196, footnote 433.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I will now go to try to check that at the next break. Thank you for clarifying. At transcript page 41347, you stated: "Communications systems were mostly obsolete. They consisted mainly of the assets of the former JNA, and these communications systems did not make it possible to have realtime communication. Superior commanders received a picture of the situation on the ground, mainly through reports from lower commanders." The statement is not true because from the very beginning - and I'm referring May 1992 - each VRS corps was required to provide oral reports to the VRS Main Staff twice a day through a secure line in addition to the written reports by the various commands; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said is correct. This part refers to the comms between the operations level and the Main Staff. I was speaking generally about the system of communications at all levels of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P3057.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 13 May 1992 order from General Milovanovic based on an oral order from General Mladic. It requires each corps to call the VRS Main Staff on a secure line twice a day; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And I did see that requirement at several places, and a relationship defined in that way between the operations level and the Main Staff so I'm not disputing that type of communication between the operational and the strategic levels.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Just so I know, have you ever seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And this requirement of reporting is mentioned in other documents as well. Daily reporting requirement. But they don't always say that it would be the personal contact between the commander of the Main Staff and the corps command, but in their absence it could be the chief of the Main Staff or the corps' Chief of Staff or the duty operations team at the corps because sometimes there would be situations when either the commander or the chiefs of staff of the corps were not personally present. But there was communications between these two levels. There was a reporting requirement twice a day, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution also please have Exhibit D333.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What we discussed -- if I'm not mistaken that the translation into English contains a mistake. The name of the -- of Manojlo Milovanovic is translated as Milanovic by mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Hopefully that was not my ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is an order from the 65th -- command of the 65th Protection Regiment dated 23 December 1993. Again, it's based on a verbal order by the chief of the Main Staff of the VRS, regarding reports. It states that there should be written regular combat reports and "in future, regular reports will not be written but the regiment Chief of Staff will call Colonel Miletic on the telephone ... every day at 0800 hours and 1900 hours ..." on a specific extension. This is another example of oral reporting that was done between the subordinate commands and the Main Staff; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are staff units that had the same requirement as the corps command, as the command at the operational level. Yes, that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 1D05358. Oh, if I could please go to page 239 in the B/C/S and page 241 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your report, in the first paragraph of your summary and conclusions, paragraph 6.0, you state: "It is difficult to rationally and objectively explain the roots of the hatred between Muslims and Orthodox Serbs. It is a historical fact that almost all Muslims (Bosniaks) in the territory of BH and of the former Yugoslavia are too [sic] too are of Serbian ethnic origin and that only Islam, as a religion, separated them from the essence of their national being. Encumbered by the syndrome of conversion and co-operation with the occupying regime of the Ottoman Empire, exposed to the scorn of their Serb brethren and compatriots, they sought a new identity. Over time, this need for being different increased and during and after the civil war in BH, it became even more pronounced, through an attempt to revise historical facts and destroy everything that they had in common with the Serbs, primarily the past, language, culture and similar." Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not just my statement. This is a position that is based on historical facts and I stand behind every word that is stated here. Yes, yes, I stand by it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, would you please avoid saying that this is not just your statement. This is your statement as put to you, and you stand by it. Whether others share it was not asked. And apart from that, but I'm perhaps also looking at Defence, it seems to be expert opinion which is beyond the field of expertise of this witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just want go to one more related comment before I ask you some documents. Could the Prosecution please have page 185 in the B/C/S and page 187 in the English. At the end of paragraph 5.11 of your report, where you are discussing the importance of the Podrinje for Serbs, you state: "An obvious example is the so-called Bosniak language, which essentially does not exist as such but is part of the Serbian language. Under political influence many terms from the Croatian language have been forcibly introduced into that language. Such subordination and domination are elements of the imposition of a cultural paradigm which is not historically intrinsic to Muslims, whose biological roots are in the Serbian people." Do you stand by this statement?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I take it these were also the views of General Radinovic, which is who you cite in footnotes 473; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We discussed this issue a number of times.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you teach this view about Muslims to your students?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I convey it to them in the same way, in lectures; also in my studies, in my books.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P6647 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In that footnote, Witness, you refer to Mr. Radinovic's testimony in Belgrade. Could you tell what testimony it was and what case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't a testimony. It was a conversation between two people. I said that I have known him for decades. I have a friendly relationship with General Radinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Because the footnote reads testimony. But it's a conversation. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: These are the SRK guide-lines from Colonel Luka Dragicevic who at this time was the assistant commander in SRK for morale, religious and legal affairs. In the fifth paragraph, the guide-lines state: "Our task is to strengthen the combat morale of our soldiers and officers, and to build up confidence in our own compatibilities and in the excellence of Serbian arms. Yes, we are genetically stronger, better, more handsome, and cleverer. Try to remember how many Muslims there were among the top ten pupils, students or soldiers. Only a few. Why? Because they are poturice and only the weakest of the Serbs became poturice. A solid and well thought out punch on the nose would make them change their fate once again." Do you share these views?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Quite the contrary. Everything that I said speaks of the same genetic national entity. We're talking about the same people who became different on the basis of their faith.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat his last sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's one people, two different faiths, and because of that faith, a new ethnic group was created. These are facts, these are things that date back 500 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I put it to you that General Dragicevic --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the translator asked for part of it to be repeated and I think Mr. Weber may have missed that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please read in the transcript where it was. Because it was already a few lines ago, Mr. Weber, if you would -- so that you guide the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you were saying in response to when I asked you whether or not you shared the views expressed by Colonel Dragicevic. You were answering and saying we were talking about the same people who became different on the basis of their faith. And then, did you say something else after that? If so, could you repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, I said that I not share these views and they are contrary to what was said in the positions presented previously. I said that this is one people with two faiths. And then those of the Islamic faith, a new ethnic group was created, first of all, during the Communist era. They were Muslims, and then after or in the course of this war, they became Bosniaks. So, these are historical facts and they can be looked at when you look at history dating 500 years back.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Colonel Dragicevic is using derogatory language towards the Muslim people in order to advocate subordinates to use violence against them; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could you repeat the name of the Colonel just for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Dragicevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not share these views. I do not support them and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, that wasn't my question. I was asking you about Colonel Dragicevic. Colonel Dragicevic is using derogatory language towards Muslim people in order to advocate his subordinates to use violence against them; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are derogatory terms, and they are inappropriate. They're inappropriately used. They're historically incorrect. And I'm not able to say what were the motives for him to use them. They are incorrect and using them is irresponsible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Before we continue, may I take you back for a second to the expert testimony on Srebrenica by Mr. Radinovic. You said it was a conversation, not testimony. You refer, however, to page 14, which suggests that there is any document made on the basis of that conversation. Is there; and are you willing to share it with us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We didn't dwell on that too much yesterday, the analysis. We did exchange opinions. We talked. We did not draft any kind of a formal document. There is no document as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But in footnote 473, you were referring to page 14. Now, how could page 14 exist if there's no document? I just -- it reads: Radovan Radinovic, military expert testimony on Srebrenica, Belgrade, 2010, page 14." And I asked you previously about in what case that testimony was. You said it was just a conversation. Now I'm asking you where we can find page 14, and you say there is no document, which puzzles me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, you were telling me about a part of it, without me seeing the document so I wasn't even aware which footnote we were talking about. That footnote refers to his personal text about Srebrenica. I don't know whether he was preparing a book, so that was material in preparation for it, but it's his personal text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you refer to it in a footnote, then that suggests that it was available to you and that the reader can check the accuracy of your conclusions or opinions on the basis of this footnote reference. Do you have that text?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will take a look to see if I have it in electronic form, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And are you willing to share it with us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, I'm going to see if I have it on my laptop in electronic form. And if I do, of course, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. Yes, I was just checking whether I had been unclear as to the footnotes. Well, it was clearly introduced as a citation in footnote 473, so, therefore, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Let me just draw the attention of the witness to his bibliography as annexed to his report. Item 59, it says: "Radovan Radinovic [B/C/S spoken]," translated as military expert testimony on Srebrenica, D160, whatever that mean, Belgrade, 2000. In footnote 473, there's a reference to the year 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As there is in some of the previous footnotes as well, there's always a reference is to 2010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I just wanted to draw the attention of this witness to this fact when checking his documents and providing us with more details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33449.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have been informed that possibly material you're looking for is from the 2000 Krstic report of Mr. Radinovic. If that assists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know. We asked the witness to clarify 2000 against 2010 whether it's evidence or he said it was a conversation just -- we'll hear from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, I want to look at two documents together. This is a 21 February 1993 SRK command order related to the presentation of the SRK combat readiness analysis for the period of 4 April to 31 December 1992. According to the first paragraph, this event would take place at 0900 hours on 27 February 1993. This would have been the first SRK combat readiness analysis during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The responsibility for providing the closing remarks at such an important event would fall upon the commander of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, General Galic at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, usually according to regulation, it would be the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, just while we still have it in our minds, I've checked the B/C/S original. Footnote 473 has the date 2000 not 2010, so the English translation has a scribner's error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would that be true for the other footnotes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't know. You didn't give the numbers so I couldn't check any further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'll have a look at it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I don't know if you completed your answer. You said: Well, usually according to regulation, it would be the commander ... You're referring to the commander of the corps; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the corps commander, the unit commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is it released, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the delayed answer is it now is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I didn't mean to build in suspense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the closing speech which in the first line refers to the first analysis of the combat readiness of the SRK. The speech was provided to the Office of the Prosecutor by General Galic's Defence in 2001. You agree that this relates to the combat readiness presentation that we looked at in the last document; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Under the third point, it states: "Our priority is that we must strive for further and full application of the hitherto to criterion of success. The value of each individual and each unit is the measure in which they have safe-guarded the Serbs and Serbian territory and how many poturice they have liquidated and how much of their territory they have seized." This is also another example, like we looked at in the last document, of using such derogatory language to encourage violence against Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This first part of this statement, in terms of controlling the territory and the protection of the Serbian people, is all right. The second part, which uses the pejorative term "poturice," Turkish convert, is not all right. But, unfortunately, it was part of the terminology used in the civil war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You agree it would be really irresponsible for a corps commander to be using such language at such an important event like the presentation of an annual combat readiness event; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That second part, I believe, is inappropriate. The one speaking about Poturice and Turkish territory, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ters 33449 and 33460 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33449 receives exhibit number P7679. 65 ter number 33460 receives exhibit number P7680, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Both are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's turn to Sarajevo and see if we can agree on a simple standard military definition of a siege. A siege is a military blockade of an area where actions are taken to force those inside the besieged area to either surrender or capitulate; right.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In our terminology of the art of war, siege and blockade are two different things. These are not synonyms.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. A siege is a holding of an area where actions are taken - so something more than just a blockade - to force those inside the besieged area to either surrender or capitulate; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly where the difference lies. Blockade does not force those who are inside either to surrender or to leave that place. Neither the civilian population nor the military forces, if it's a defended city. And that's where the difference lies between siege in its archaic and medieval meaning and blockade as a legitimate military action taken and accepted by all armies.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 4.56 of your report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before we do that, Mr. Weber, I'm not quite sure that the witness accepts your definition of siege in any way. I mean, now that you defined it without using the word "blockade." Can we hear from the witness do you agree with the definition as reformulated, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'll just it give one quick chance to see if maybe I can break it down simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you agree a siege involves military forces holding an area?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That they holding an area, yes. But you also put other elements in the definition which do not correspond to the blockade. That is, forcing the population and military forces, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... the area that they hold, you agree, surrounds the besieged area; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Geographically, the space is such that you can say that they are encircling it and Sarajevo was never encircled. I mean, the Muslim part of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm just going step by step to see if we can agree on the concepts. The area what is encircled then by the forces, there are then actions taken to force those inside that area to either surrender or capitulate; right? And I'm leaving it broad because there are different types of actions that could be taken.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will object to the question as being vague because we're talking about vagueties [sic]. If we're talking about a military expert and expertise, there are texts, there are military texts, there are military sources that give definitions. I used some in direct. I don't see why the Prosecution is using vague terminology. Actions, what kind of actions? Why don't we talk about specifics here? Instead of at hour five of the cross-examination, we're talking about vagueties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm trying to agree on a basic definition. And I -- we'll get to many different actions here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, do not interrupt Mr. Ivetic when making an objection. If you say you'll further specify perhaps you could do it the other way around.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First, pay attention to specific actions and see if you can agree on any definition. Apart from that, of course, this Chamber is primarily interested in the facts rather than whether you could qualify them as A, B or C, because it's not the qualification, it's the factual situation that will guide us primarily. But, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let me try this a different way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of paragraph 4.56 of your report, you state that General Michael Rose said in his book that Sarajevo had not been a besieged city. I take it you referenced General Rose on this point because he is clearly someone of such military experience that he would certainly know whether or not Sarajevo was even under siege; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the meaning in which I used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33442 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you referred to paragraph 4.56 of the report. Can you verify, please, the number. I don't know find such a paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Page 124, Your Honours. In English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: It's at the very end of the paragraph, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is General Rose's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 18 which is the first page of the text of the introduction to the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: General Rose's book starts: "When I arrived Sarajevo at night-fall on the 23 January 1994, it had been a city under siege for two years and seemed deserted. Amid the rubble of shattered buildings, its 350.000 inhabitants were living like rats in cellars, only venturing out at night to search for their means of survival. Sarajevo was where the war had started but would not end." Did you read the very first paragraph of General Rose's book?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not read this paragraph. Of course, in drafting my military expert report, I used people who knew English well, and who found this passage regarding his view of the siege. This passage here I'm not disputing it. It was his personal feeling on the day or the night when he arrived there. And I can also add that Sarajevo looked like a ghost town ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 46 of the book.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do so -- Do I understand that English texts you're relying on that you didn't read them yourself or that you relied on others who had read it for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Because my main second language is Russian. I know English only at beginning -- beginner's level. Very basic understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please go to page 46 of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll read the paragraph. It's the third paragraph on this page, where General Rose says: "I might as well have saved my breath. The next morning, the headlines in the local newspaper, the Oslobodjenje, reported that I did not consider the citizens of Sarajevo to be under siege. Neier also wrote to the Secretary-General of the UN urging him to order me to 'reverse' my plan to redeploy observers from their task of counting shells, as this procedure kept the international spotlight on the attacks that were being mounted." This is the part of the book that you mean to reference in your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The next paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I put on the record that the footnote actually refers to two pages although Mr. Weber has only shown one.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. I just wanted to know if it was a part of the book.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The next paragraph --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the part of the book that is cited is two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So you are misstating the footnote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not all at the same time. I think the footnote states page 40, page 41 and apparently that's a reference to the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm -- Your Honours, I think that I cannot locate any other similar part besides this part in the English version. So I did try to look for those pages. If counsel has other pages he would like me to refer to I'd be happy to hear from him over the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He mentioned page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: But, Your Honour, if I may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The next paragraph General Rose states: "It was clear to me that this adverse publicity against me in my time in command could prove disastrous. So I immediately called a meeting with the prime minister, Haris Silajdzic, and explained to him that whoever had reported my views to the ... papers had got it wildly wrong."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "To the local papers."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "...to the local papers had got it wildly wrong. What I had actually said was that I did not want to develop a siege mentality and that I wished to live in Sarajevo like any other citizen."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were looking at General Rose's or when you had General Rose's statements referred to you did you consider whether or not he had actually repudiated them or rejected them in his own book?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From this, we can clearly see the political but also the media influence on the stances of General Rose. I think that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... would you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am trying to answer. Could he then put the question more precisely?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Weber it was a pretty precise question but perhaps you repeat it, Mr. Weber, so as to assist the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you were considering the statements of General Rose in his book, did you further consider whether or not he had rejected them, any statements or qualified them any statements in the book itself?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there are two statements, I took the one that is closer to my understanding of the situation in the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 50.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On this page, in the third paragraph, General Rose describes his views of General Mladic. In the paragraph, General Rose states Mladic: "Had a reputation among his soldiers for bravery and success in the fighting that took place in 1991 in the Krajina region of Croatia. For him, the dominant role of battle was the attack. He was revered by his soldiers for his habit of jumping into a tank and leading from the front. He was also deeply religious and once told me that he prayed every day for the lives of his men. Nevertheless, he saw nothing wrong in using terror as a weapon or civilians as targets for his artillery if this advanced his strategy. Mladic suffered rapid changes of mood and used a combination of persuasion, trickery and intimidation to win arguments." You do not refer to General Rose's impression of General Mladic and his willingness to use terror in your report, do you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the position of General Rose. I do not share that opinion and it never occurred to me to include it in my report. I believe, on top of it, that it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Did you review the 16th Assembly Session of the Serbian Republic on 12 May 1992? You referred to this in paragraph 2.49 of your report.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we display it? Of course I did, if it's in the paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P431, page 35 in the B/C/S and page 43 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that. For the record it should be clear that Mr. Weber that you were always referring to e-court pages of the book of General Rose; whereas, apparently the witness in his footnotes, correctly or not, is referring to hard copy pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for clarifying that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Because page 50 in e-court is page 33 in the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Before you is General Mladic's speech at the 16th Assembly Session. At the bottom of the page before you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And Your Honours, this is the middle of the page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: General Mladic states: "With artillery, I will clear the path for the soldiers. What I do care? I do not have to go down Volunteer Street. I shell them until I have driven him crazy. Once we have driven him crazy, he will either flee of his own accord or, he does not even have to run away. Once we have approached we will capture him, and let us not play the game of taking prisoners." General Mladic was willing to shell individuals in order to drive them crazy; right? That's what he says in his own words.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that way as you are putting it. It's a pejorative term for the effect of action against people who are defending themselves, who are in the course of accomplishing missions. It's classical neutralisation of the target.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to go on a new topic. If we can take the break at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
