utterances.text: Yes. But before we do that, a few lines further down it also says, "and let's not play the game of taking prisoners." Any comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think we can look at two words outside of the context. This discusses a situation of one ambush after another against units of the -- the VRS as was done in Dobrovoljacka Street while the JNA was withdrawing. I don't know in which other context I should interpret these words.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that comment. You may follow the usher. Mr. Ivetic, if it would help you in any way on the footnotes on the testimony whether it's -- we referred to, first of all, 473 where you say the original says 2000. Could I draw your attention to 472 where, in the B/C/S, it says 2010. To footnote 469, where it says 2010 as well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- in the B/C/S. And then to 468 where, in the B/C/S, it reads 2002, whereas in the English, no year is referred to at all. That -- I don't know who prepared the translation of the -- is it a CLSS translation which might then need to be -- to some extent be corrected? Well, I leave it in your hands at this moment. We take a break and resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber apologises for the late re-start. The witness can be escorted in the courtroom. Meanwhile, I'll briefly deal with Exhibit P3096 which is a SRK combat report, which was admitted into evidence on the 12th of December, 2013. On the 11th of November of this year, the Prosecution e-mailed the Chamber and the Defence advising that: 1, in the first paragraph of the translation, "Runjevica facility" should read "Runjevica feature," and 2, a revised translation had been uploaded into e-court under doc ID 0620-1092-1 ET. The Defence responded on the 12th of November, stating that it did not object to the replacement of the translation. The Chamber hereby instructs the Registry to replace the English translation of the P3096 with the revised one. Mr. Weber, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Diverzantsko-teroristicka grupa, also known as DTG units, are manned with snipers; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which part of the text or which event we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm speaking generally. DTG groups are manned with snipers. You mentioned them at various points throughout your report.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. The composition and the equipment for sabotage and terrorist groups would be defined by the action they would be carrying out, so it's not always true that they would also have snipers.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P4517, page 6 of the B/C/S and page 9 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is the 31 May 1993 VRS Main Staff assessment related to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. In the bottom paragraph before you, the assessment states: "The activities of ..." And in the original, it says: "Diverzantsko-teroristicka grupa should be used in further operations, as well as ambushes and surprise activities, so that there is a constant negative effect on the morale of the Muslim forces and population. That they have a sense of fear and constant insecurity from the activities of our forces." Sir, I put to you that it was the instruction of the VRS Main Staff for the SRK to use DTG groups to instill a sense of fear against the civilian position of Sarajevo and not just the Muslim forces; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just see the beginning of this document. Actually, can I see the beginning of the document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, did you hear the request --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't if know the witness can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I mean, you put to the witness what the document is and if the witness asks to find -- to have a look at it, then you should give it to him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I asked to see the beginning of the document because this term, "sabotage terrorist groups," for the most part in the doctrine literature and documents of the JNA was used to designate parts of enemy groups that infiltrated one's own area of combat. That's why I asked to look at the beginning. All the groups that were infiltrated into the enemy disposition were called sabotage groups, or reconnaissance groups. And that's why I believe that this paragraph that you indicated, in the military sense, is incorrectly written and from my own personal professional point of view, was not properly presented, either as -- in terms of the contents or the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is -- this relates to the VRS forces. This is a VRS document. In the recommendation, the instruction that's in it relates to the DTG groups of the VRS; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm not disputing that that's what it says. But I think that that is not in keeping with the doctrinary practice and I think there is an error made by the person who drafted the document. They could have talked about sabotage groups but not about sabotage terrorist groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. The -- the fact is, is that the SRK used snipers to terrorise the civilian population of Sarajevo. You're aware of that; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in that way, no. In my report, I stated findings about the use of snipers by both of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Oh, okay. So what I'm asking is simply about one of the warring parties. The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps used snipers to instill a sense of fear into the civilian population of Sarajevo. You are aware that; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33361.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a 11 April 1993 ABiH document you reference in footnote 356 of your report, under section A, related to the SRK's grouping of forces. The document shows that the SRK had snipers nests in the area of Grbavica; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only in the area of Grbavica. Snipers were deployed there along the entire line of the front, stretching 240 kilometres. Here, they're being put in the context only of the inner part of old town but they were also deployed in the urban areas of the city, on both sides. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 33361 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33361 receives exhibit number P7681, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No objections. Therefore, admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4.148 of your report, you indicate: "Although the greatest responsibility for civilian casualties in the Muslim part of Sarajevo lies with the authorities and commands in the Muslim part of the city, the civilian population failed to comply with the necessary safety measures that are implicit in an area that has become a battle-field." At the end of the paragraph, by way of illustration, you refer to a single sentence from a United Nations report from UNMO Cutler. You did not consider all the relevant information from this document when you were drafting your report; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean when you say "all the relevant information."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you feel that you considered all the relevant information from this report when presenting your analysis in your own report.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This conclusion was formulated in that manner, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33452.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the report that you referenced in the footnote, the -- Colonel Cutler's 2nd January 1993 report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we go to page 3, please, and focus on paragraph 8.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 8, we see the sentence you quote in your report. It's in the middle of the paragraph. It states: "However, the resilience of the Sarajevo people continues to amaze me. Most go about their daily business as if there was no war." Did you read the beginning of this paragraph about the conditions of the hospitals in Sarajevo or the part -- following sentence where it states "there is no question that much of the population would not survive without the enormous air and road lift -- air and road lift of the UNHCR humanitarian aid that comes in." Did you read those parts?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to the first page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And on this page in the second paragraph, the UN report states: "On the eve of the summit talks on the situation in BiH, there's an uneasy calm laying over the besieged and sorrowful city of Sarajevo. Snow lays on the ground in the city as it enters the 24th day without electricity or water." When you were reaching your conclusions about civilians going out into public and exposing themselves to fire, you did not consider that they may have needed to go outside due to the lack of utilities or to obtain humanitarian aid to survive, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must also note the fact that Sarajevo is a city where I grew up, where I completed high school, and I know completely that all these facts are relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. If you knew that they were relevant, you don't mention any of these facts in your consideration of why civilians were caught out in the open during the war; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so. I wanted to go on to say that Sarajevo, as a city here in this report, is just being -- the part that is being looked at is the old part of the town, the central part. The same applied to the rest of the town which was under Serb control, the citizens of Vogosca and Ilidza lived in exactly the same conditions. So the same description would apply to the way they lived also. That's why I am mentioning it. The life of the civilian population in the Serbian and the Muslim parts of the city was equally difficult and equally tragic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your paragraph relates to the Muslim part of Sarajevo. So what I'm asking you, sir, is the fact that you did not consider in your analysis of the Muslim part of Sarajevo of why civilians were caught out in the open, the fact that they might had to go out to get humanitarian aid or just water to survive; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean, when you say to go out. You mean to leave the city which was under a blockade? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No. I mean to go outside of their homes.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, everybody had a need to do that. They did have the need for that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 33452 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33452 receives exhibit number P7682, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Witness, could I ask you, in paragraph 4.148 you say these civilians were behaving irresponsibly, where going out, going to work was already dangerous. How do you know when people were moving around, why they did that? And why do you say that going to work is dangerous that you should have stayed inside for other reasons. Could you tell us what your basis of knowledge is why all those people moving around were out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is being discussed here is the line of contact. We're talking about the population that was in the area of contact and in the combat disposition area of units at the front. This is the direct line of contact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... my question was about a different thing. You write in your report: They unnecessarily went out. How do you know whether it was necessary or not to go out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This does not refer to the entire city. It only refers to the confrontation line which was in the inner area of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, that's not what you write in your report. You say the civilian population failed to comply with the necessary safety measures that are implicit in an area that has become a battle-field. By this, we mean unnecessary movements, taking walks, any groupings or loitering in the areas at risk. We've seen evidence of persons trying to fetch water out of their homes in an area where they were not safe. So is it your position that they should have stayed inside without water and not have gone out and not to group behind the bridge because they considered that, perhaps, the safest place to get that water? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, that is not my position. And I did not express myself that way. I'm speaking about the zone or the immediate zone next to the area of conflict. The military authorities and the military units were supposed to release the civilian population from those areas so that they would not fall victims there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But you are blaming the civilian population, not only authorities, but you are clearly distinguishing between the responsibility of the authorities and the civilian population failed to comply with the necessary safety measures by going out, unnecessarily. If you happen to live close to where a confrontation line was, do you think you should stay inside and then be without water? Is that what the population should have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. The population in the area of the front where the military units were deployed should have been moved out. That would be the best way to reduce the suffering of the civilian population and possible casualties.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's fine that you say that. But that's not what your report tells us. Do you agree that are you blaming the population itself for failing to take the -- comply with the safety measures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Quite the contrary. Later, in several places, I do say that the commands were supposed to do that together with the authorities, to move the civilians out of those areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, I note for the record that the rest of the paragraph which you didn't read talks about confrontation line and talks about commands, rather than moving people out, encouraging mass gathering in the confrontation line. So I think the question posed by Your Honour is misleading as to the text in the report because it is in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I read literally from the report the portion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's in the same paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, again, please don't interrupt me. If you think that further questions should be put to the witness to give the proper context then have you an opportunity to do so in re-examination. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4.16 of your report, you discuss a number of things but amongst them you talk about Islamic religious facilities and cultural centres that paint the picture of Sarajevo as an Islamic city and how it was no longer a multi-ethnic city but one of the largest Islamic cities and Islamic cultural centres in Europe. You also describe how the Muslim houses have been restored and how the Serb parts are left burned. When was the last time you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have been there for the past three years. Each year consecutively.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You agree that's still much visible war damage to many of the buildings throughout the entire city? Areas that were held by both ABiH forces and also VRS forces.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I noticed were just odd parts that were damaged on certain high-rise buildings. The houses that were demolished, including my own house, have not been rebuilt. They have been left as they were, and it's been 20 years now since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33439 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Weber, there seems to be a small e-court crash which needs to be repaired before we can continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. The remainder of the material that I do have to go through before handing over to Mr. McCloskey relates to documents in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I don't know how much time it takes to get back to a functioning e-court system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll be informed about how much time that takes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think if we take an early break because it will certainly take a couple of minutes to have it function again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe Ms. Stewart might be able to do a little magic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to give it a try we understood that in approximately five minutes the e-court problems would be over. If we could continue on that basis, then let's give it a try. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just for the record, this is displaying 65 ter 33439. If footnote 327 of your report, you reference the final report of the expert commission established pursuant to Security Council resolution 780, number S/1994/674. Before us, are appendices 4 and 5 to the report which can he see referenced at the top of the page with the same number. Did you review these appendices, when you were preparing your report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Appendix 4 provides an overview of the most frequently hit targets and dates when the shellings were recorded. Do you agree that areas including the down-town city centre --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could scroll down on the page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- Ilidza, old town, Bascarsija, and on the next page, I believe even Dobrinja appears. Do you agree that these areas -- that these areas were regularly shelled, subjected to shelling, starting in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We see here areas both under Serb and under Muslim control. And what "regularly" means, I don't know. But that there was mutual action, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please go to page 6 of the document which will be appendix 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: There is the appendix describes over 50 Muslim cultural and religious structures that were damaged by shelling during the war. You agree that Muslim cultural and religious structures shelled -- were shelled in Sarajevo and many sustained substantial damage during the conflict; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many. I don't know what that adjective means. Some were --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... over 50.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the exact number. But many of them were occupied as military-use buildings, I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to that you there's nothing in this document that indicates that. We're not really able to flip through it right now, but I think can you even see from the heading that there's no information on it.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean that they were used as military buildings?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders this document into evidence, 65 ter 33439. If we could reserve a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives exhibit number P7683, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I do not know if e-court is back up? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I more precisely should have said that number is reserved because it's not available in e-court, whereas I used the term "marked for identification."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It will take at least ten more minutes. Perhaps it would be wiser to take the break first and have a functioning system after the break. We'll take a break and we'd like to see you back in 20 minute, Mr. Kovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll resume at quarter past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we -- wait for one second. First of all, Madam Registrar, is the e-court functioning again? It apparently is functioning again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to raise a matter. The Chamber would like to come back to a comment made by Mr. Ivetic before the break. Mr. Ivetic, you blamed the Presiding Judge having misled the witness by putting his question to him. On behalf of Judge Moloto, I have to reject this allegation. First, it shows a wrong interpretation of what the Presiding Judge put to the witness. Judge Orie literally quoted from the witness report and asked the witness for his comment. To qualify this as misleading is wrong and unacceptable. Second, it is inappropriate to criticise a judge in this way. Mr. Ivetic, you should think about your language. If you want to come back to the Chamber not immediately but after having thought about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I must just add that, in fact, there was no basis for that criticism.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be -- I think Judge Fluegge - and I don't take the primary role here - invited you to think it over and then to address the matter again if you wish. Therefore, I would previous that the witness is escorted in the courtroom now. If you wouldn't -- if you wanted to address the matter, Mr. Ivetic, but I'm consulting Judge Fluegge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have an opportunity. That's at least what my colleague considers a wise thing to do, you have an opportunity to do that at the end of this session. We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Kovac, in writing the Sarajevo section of your report, you refer to many documents from the ABiH. I'm going to go through a few more of them with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33358 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a document you reference in footnote 333 of your report. It is a 9 January 1994 ABiH 102nd MBR order for engineering support for defence. It has the same sequential number as the document in your footnote. Directing your attention to the second paragraph of item 1, which relates to VRS actions, it states: "They have shown maximum savagery in operations so far, destroying the city, killing civilian inhabitants, and using them in some cases as human shields." The ABiH materials that you reviewed for your case showed and discussed the fact that the VRS was destroying the city, killing civilians, and, in some cases, using them even as human shields; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's correct, especially this part referring to human shields. I don't know what the author of that passage meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, sir, my question was more basic. I'm not really even asking whether or not you agree with this or not. I'm just asking that's -- that was information related to the destruction of the city and the killing of civilians that were in the materials that you reviewed; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's inaccurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33358 receives exhibit number P7684, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Mr. Weber, before the break, you have shown through Sanction on the screen 65 ter 33439 for which P7683 was reserved. Is it -- it is released, I take it, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then 65 ter 33439 is now receiving P7683.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe that the -- okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I misspoke. 76 -- no. 7683 was reserved for it and is now admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4.81 of your report, you discuss the artillery ability of the ABiH and reference one ABiH document from 12 March 1993. You indicate that the document claims: "Operations Group Igman has a 152 M84 Nora Howitzer and a 152 D-20 Howitzer," and then you include an ellipse. You do not give an exactly accurate depiction of the information in the document and the ABiH's ability to use these weapons, did you?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that relates to only one part of the front line: The outer ring of the Sarajevo theatre of war. And it relates to large-calibre weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You feel that you gave an accurate impression of the ABiH's ability to use these weapons from the document in your report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far from it. It refers only to some large-calibre weapons. It does not reflect the entire artillery of the 1st Corps of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's get to the heart of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33451 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the document from OG Igman that you cite in your report. The first paragraph indicates that the shells corresponded to the wrong type of Howitzer. And the full sentence, which you quote, states: "Operations Group Igman was a 152 M84 Nora Howitzer and a 152 D- 20, and the available shells can not be used unless previously improved." You left this latter part off of your report and inserted an ellipse to conceal the fact that the ABiH could not use the shells for these Howitzers; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not right. It's the same weapon of Russian and Yugoslav manufacture. The only difference was in the length of the hull, the casing, and it can be solved in the work-shop and it was solved very easily so that second part of the sentence really has no significance. That was just the situation at one moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You only cite one document in the paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution will tender 65 ter 33451 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33451 receives exhibit number P7685, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33364.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is an ABiH combat readiness assessment that you appear to cite on multiple occasions in your report. In the top half of the page before -- actually, if we could go to page 2 of the B/C/S and page 3 of the English translation. In the top half of the page before you, the assessment discusses the ability of the VRS to control the city with artillery and then states: "Through such a firing system, the efficient use of our forces in offensive combat has been greatly disabled ..." The paragraph does go on to note achievements in the area of Zuc. You acknowledge that the ABiH's offensive ability had been greatly disabled by the VRS artillery during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's a fact that VRS had stronger artillery forces numerically, but BH army had better conditions for camouflaging their artillery weapons inside the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders the document 65 ter 33464 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 33464 receives exhibit number P7686, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4.56, you state: "It should be borne in mind that the Blue Routes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, could you please check whether the document really bears 65 ter number 33464 or was it 33364?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. It's 65 ter 33364.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And that document has now been admitted as P7686. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 4.56, you state: "It should be borne in mind that the Blue Routes supplying the city with humanitarian relief functioned throughout the war." In paragraph 4.62 of your report, you state that: "It should also be borne in mind in all of the periods of the war, RS and its army, the VRS, always allowed the passage of humanitarian relief convoys for the civilian population." Your assertions that the Blue Routes functioned throughout the war and that the VRS always allowed the passage of humanitarian aid are false. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they're not false. Blue convoys always passed except in periods when transports were discovered to carry ammunition and explosives. That's when delays occurred in the passage of humanitarian aid because cases with shells, ammunition, and other lethal assets destined for the ABiH were discovered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31182 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 15 March 1995 UNPROFOR memorandum containing a chronology of events for the Blue Routes during their existence. It doesn't mention any of the things that you just mentioned but I will go through a bunch of the entries for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 in both versions. I'm going to redact my last comment. In fact, it does mention it as a reason that was given by the Bosnian Serbs during the course of the events.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The first entry relates to a 17 March 1994 agreement to establish the Blue Routes. Under entry for 26 July 1994 we see that Radovan Karadzic informs UNPROFOR of the cancellation of the agreement on the passage of traffic across the airport and he blames the Muslim activities as the reason, some of the ones that that you just described. We see on the next date that the roads across the airport were closed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have the next page in both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of the entry for 11 January 1995, related to a series of meetings, there's reference to implementation of modalities from 17 March 1994 with the intention of opening the routes no later than 14 January 1995. At the end of that the entry for 15 January, which is on the next page, this chronology indicates the roads remained closed. This chronology does indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Next page in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This chronology does indicate that between 1 February 1995, the airport routes were opened to international organisations and then later opened to civilian traffic on 6 February 1995. The Sarajevo-Visoko route, according to this, was opened on 10 February and then closed on 25 February 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Next page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if we could go to the final entries. The one related to the 12th of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you give good guidance --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Last page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- as to where to proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Second-to-last page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see according to the 11 March entry that after the sniping of two Serb girls, the Blue Routes were closed then on 12 March 1995. So, first of all, based on this chronology, the fact is that there were substantial periods that the Blue Routes were not open during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think that's true. I think this states precisely the reasons and arguments supporting my previous assertion. There was sniping by Muslim forces and the abuse of humanitarian convoys to transport ammunition and weapons. If this was raised to the level of president, that means that these violations were rather frequent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I put it to that you the Bosnian Serb forces, the VRS, closed the Blue Routes, for example, on this last occasion in retaliation for a sniping event. They were willing to do that; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not retaliation. It was a regular action. If you let through a humanitarian convoy and Muslim forces go on to snipe, that's a causal relationship between these two things. Because that was the route of the convoy, the humanitarian convoy. Maybe somebody was trying to obstruct the passage of humanitarian convoys, somebody from the special force, special Muslim forces in Sarajevo. That's how I see it. If somebody is receiving humanitarian aid it's not logical for them to kill two young girls in that same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 31182 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It receives exhibit number P7687, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. It is admitted into evidence. Witness could you tell us where these two Serbs were killed, apart from Grbavica, what special location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They were killed all over the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's specifically this report --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, these two girls could not have been killed all over the city. I'm asking you about where these two girls were killed. More specifically than only Grbavica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not look into the location of every killing but I know the area, the points where killings took place in the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not write an expert report on the killing of these two girls. But it is a fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You said because that was the route of the convoy. Not knowing where they were killed, it -- I need further explanation as why they were killed at the route of the convoy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not talking precisely about the street, but it's -- it was on the route of the convoy, its entry from the direction of Nedzarici towards Stup and towards old town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now Grbavica, is that on the road between Nedzarici and the old town.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The quickest route from Nedzarici to the old town is not on the side of the Miljacka river where Grbavica is, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on the opposite bank but these are parallel roads along the river, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You say it's close enough. I have another question for you. You are talking about smuggling of explosives and ammunition and the Chamber has heard evidence about that over limited number of occasions. How many of these occasions happened, in your view, which would explain that the Blue Routes were not used temporarily? How many incidents of the smuggling are you aware of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was a cause-and-effect relationship. I think that was for the only reason for delays or for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, why don't you answer my question? My question is: How many incidents of smuggling ammunition and explosives through convoys of humanitarian aid are known to you? Is it two or three? Is it ten? Is it 20? Please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Approximate number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Around ten times that I know of. But I did not try to determine the number. I dealt with the occurrence. It was already a regular activity and a problem for the -- the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say it's a regular activity, then the number is relevant, isn't it, because that makes it either regular or incidental.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If it's several times including the number that I mentioned, it's a regular occurrence in the four years of war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Ivetic, if in re-examination -- I have a recollection of a few incidents. It's not my recollection that there were ten, but if there's anything there which could assist the Chamber in getting a -- a better knowledge of the -- how regular and how frequent that was that would be appreciated. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 10111 for the witness. Page 4 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 29 March 1995 UNPROFOR report. In paragraph 11 it contains information on the Blue Routes and states: "The BSA have claimed they will close the Blue Routes for 30 days for every Serb killed in the Sarajevo area." This is a threat to cut off humanitarian aid as retaliation; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not correct. Because it's a different context of the combat situation in the Sarajevo theatre of war in that inner ring. If you allow me, I'll clarify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I tender the document at this time, 65 ter 10111.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Receives exhibit number P7688, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In footnotes 339 and 340, you quote Asim Dzambasovic's Karadzic's testimony and, for the record, he testified without protective measures in that case. You quote him for the proposition that there were 60.000 soldiers in Sarajevo. Did you review all of this witness's testimony for your report?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not the entire testimony. And I also compared other data indicating that, and they are not in keeping with this particular figure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33484. If we could go to page 41.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Coming up will be a part of Mr. Dzambasovic's Karadzic testimony, a different section that the one you cite in your report. And if we could please start at line 20. In that case, Mr. Dzambasovic was asked: "Thank you. And also yesterday, in relation to your position as Chief of Staff in the 1st Corps, you were asked about the manpower of the corps, and you affirmed that it was roughly 60.000 soldiers. And I have three questions on this topic. The first is: Of that 60.000, how many were actually -- were located outside the encircled city of Sarajevo? "A. I personally think -- well, right now, I don't have the exact" --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If we could have the next page, please. "... figures here, but I think that in the city, itself, there were about 30.000 men, and that many outside the city as well. At that time, Gorazde was within the area of responsibility of the 1st Corps too, so the Army of Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the area of Gorazde, was within the 1st Corps. Also, the unit in Zepa at the time was within the 1st Corps. That is the period of 1992 and 1993. "Q. Thank you. And of the 30.000 who were inside the city, how many were located at the confrontation lines at any given time? "A. Well, approximately, it is my estimate right now - again, I cannot give you an exact figure - but I think it is between 4.000 and 5.000. "Q. Thank you. And of the 30.000 soldiers located inside the city, how many of them had weapons? "A. Well, one quarter, roughly, had weapons." You did not include this information in your report; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it's incorrect. The commander of the 1st Corps in the study that I cited provided different data regarding the number of men and weapons. That's why I said that there was several sources of information about the strength of the 1st Corps during the war, including the -- those who were inside the -- Sarajevo and those outside. So the corps commander and his Chief of Staff provided incorrect information about the number of men. I believe that the corps commander did know the information regarding his own corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This Chamber has received some evidence on these numbers before even during this time-period from witnesses who have indicated that it was not much more than this number, maybe 35.000, high 30.000s. You agree that a large amount of the 1st Corps forces were located outside of the city in what you would refer to as the external ring; correct?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is incorrect. The bulk of the 1st Corps forces were in the town, including police and special forces, and independent unit that were linked with the General Staff of the B and H army. The number that, in my opinion, applied to the town in this figure is about 30.000. At this time around 1993. I would not say that it was 4.000. The entire corps was armed. There were no unarmed soldiers, and the weapons were not passed back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 01010.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the problem is, I think, that in footnote 339, you presented as if that witness said that there were 60.000 men, right or wrong, in Sarajevo; whereas, reading the testimony, then it is clear that he intends to say that there were 30.000 in Sarajevo and 30.000 somewhere else. That's the problem. Whether he is right or wrong, because that now becomes the focus, is not really what is of concern at this moment. It may be very important. But, at this moment, the issue is that you present it as if this witness said 60.000 in Sarajevo where, when reading same page, next page, just a few lines further down, that he says it was 30.000. Again, right or wrong, but you are using a source in a way which -- well, perhaps gives us not the full information. And that's one of the concerns that are expressed by Mr. Weber, and if you want to comment on that, please, have you an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I would like to. Quite the opposite. I said that there were certainly sources of information regarding structure and strength of the 1st Corps in that period and I did present that information in the text. As far as I was concerned, the most objective information was given by the commander of the corps and his Chief of Staff in monographs that they published after the war. I did cite them in the footnotes of my report. The bulk of the forces, roughly two-thirds right until 1995 were situated in Sarajevo, in the inner area of Sarajevo, on a front of some 55 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's not really an answer to my question because I'm not saying that there are no other sources, I'm not saying whether you're right or wrong in your analysis of all those sources. What I'm saying is that the concern expressed by Mr. Weber is - and that's what I was seeking your comment on - is that you present this witness as saying that there were 60.000 in Sarajevo, whereas reading a few lines furthers down, he says there were 30.000 in Sarajevo. I leave it to that at this moment. Your comment apparently has not fully addressed the matter I raised. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, paragraph 4.39, which has the witness's calculations, precisely talks about what was in the city and outside the city. The report does not, as I read it, rely upon the numbers of 60.000 that is in the transcript citation. The transcript citation is being cited for other conclusions, and in this section 4.39, the sources for the varying estimates are given and there is a description of the forces that were outside of the city of Sarajevo so I believe if we want to have the record be full and complete, we have to read the entirety of the report, not take matters out of context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's on the record. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 1st Corps command intelligence organ report dated 14 July 1993. We see it's from Asim Dzambasovic. It indicates in item 3 that Ratko Mladic has ordered that Sarajevo is to be attacked with all available means and that panic should first be created through the use of snipers. Did you find documents like this in your review of the ABiH materials? This is not one of the ones that in your report.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not quote it because this is classic propaganda and part of media war that was being waged on the Sarajevo front. I looked at the ratio of forces, and the number of sniper weapons in the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and the 1st Corps of the B and H army, and this objective picture and the ratio of snipers would not give us this particular result.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay. You call this propaganda. We see it's an intelligence organ report that is marked "Military Secret, Strictly Confidential" and it's not sent to any media or press. I see it's sent to all brigades, OG Igman and to the files. This is a confidential document; right?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it is sent to OG Igman then there are really very little reasons for these things to be mentioned there. The --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There is no tactical need for the information referred to in paragraph 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tenders 65 ter 01010 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would ask that if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar. Yes, you want to object.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Fine --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The interpreters have asked for the witness to repeat his answer. We have not had that happen, therefore I will object at this point procedurally to admitting an exhibit without getting the evidence relating to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I thought, as a matter of fact, that the witness continued but could you please -- the interpreters -- let me see where it is exactly. Yes. You are recorded as having said: "If it is sent to OG Igman, then there are really very little reasons for these things to be mentioned there. The -- And then the interpreters missed what you said then. And I'll read to you where they resumed recording what you said. You said: "There is no tactical need for the information referred to in paragraph 3." What did you say in between these lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That the bulk of the snipers from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and from the 1st Corps were located in the inner ring as it is referred to in the documents. In the inner part of the city.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. This being completed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 01010 receives exhibit number P7689, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7689 is admitted into evidence. Witness, may I again draw your attention to really focussing on what is asked. The last question was about if you call it propaganda, how could an internal document be propaganda? Now, you may have an answer to that. I do not know. But at least you didn't give an answer to that question. If you have an answer, then please tell us what it is.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have an answer to that question. The media war was waged throughout the conflict on the Sarajevo front. Mostly it was construed by the political aspect and then it was implemented in the military operational sense. When I speak about that operational sense, I'm talking about staged, planted events that would disturb the international public and allegedly point to the barbaric actions of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the issue really raised by Mr. Weber, as I understood it, is that if you want to distribute propaganda, as you said the document was, you'd rather not do that in an internal document but do it in a press release or draw the attention of the public, rather than put that into a document which is expected not to go beyond those who are addressed. That was the issue, I think, Mr. Weber raised and which has not fully been addressed in your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me to continue. That area, the relationship towards the media, was implemented internally through command documents and by utilizing a part of the special forces of the B and H army on the Sarajevo front. Reports were provided, incidents were staged, there was sniper actions that were used for propaganda purposes. So the army and their documents were also part of this propaganda machine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I understand you well, the input in those internal documents and the effect of the activities taken on the basis of that, that are the propaganda elements rather than this to be a propaganda document itself. Is that well understood?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... yes, this third --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P4422 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the exhibit number?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 14 December 1993 supplement to VRS directive number 6 to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps. This order is from General Mladic. And in the first paragraph, he orders formations from multiple VRS corps, the MUP and VJ special forces to prevent a breakthrough towards Sarajevo from the direction of Central Bosnia and Gorazde. Just stopping here, this Chamber has received evidence that VJ forces were sent into Bosnia. Are you aware that this happened at the end of 1993 and beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I do know about those operations by the Muslim army and they were partially presented in the report both from the aspect of the composition and their objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm totally lost at what you just said. I referred to the VJ, the Yugoslav army and this is a VRS Main Staff document. I asked you whether or not you were aware that VJ special forces were sent into Bosnia at the end of 1993, beginning of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object to the question. Actually the original question referred to the breakout. I don't believe that the breakout refers to the JNA or the VRS. I believe that it refers to precisely the forces that the witness was answering as to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe my question did focus on the VJ forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If there's any misunderstanding about what your question was focussing upon, please put it again to the witness so we don't have any confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you aware that VJ special forces were sent into Bosnia end of 1993 beginning of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not the question I had earlier. Could I please have a specific question to which I can give a proper answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Witness, you're an intelligent man. You followed that Mr. Weber was invited to again put a question to you, and then there's no need to comment on the previous question because you should have understood that Mr. Weber now formulated his question so as to avoid any misunderstanding and to receive your answer, not your comment. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to many, actually according to several documents, yes, the B and H army, primarily the document or the monograph of the commander of the 1st Corps, that's where I saw the number and the manner of engagement of a portion of those forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: "Those forces," meaning VJ special force?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They explicitly mention about 30 specials from the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But just a follow-up. You are saying you read this in document of the B and H army. The question relates to not a document of the BH army but a document that comes I think from the Republika Srpska from the Army of the Main Staff saying, in fact, that VJ forces, special forces be used. This is the document on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All it says here is a different number. I'm not disputing what is stated here or what I said before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... not asking you about numbers. I'm saying you are referring to BH documents when, in fact, you are being asked about a VRS document. It is a VRS document that is saying that VJ special forces be used as part of this operation. So don't deviate from the VRS and then go and tell us about the BiH when, in fact, you are being asked about a document by the VRS. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see that it says here ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm just going to try and expedite this so we can finish for the day. We see in this supplement to the directive of -- number 6 that the end of the point 1 that there is reference to the -- to provide conditions for the division of Sarajevo into two parts, which I believe is relatively consistent with your report. And then if we could scroll down in the English, we see that the operation is to be carried out in two phases and the readiness for attack is to be on the 19th of December, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could we please have the next page in both -- both versions. According to the -- actually, I'm sorry. Might have to go back to the previous page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: We see under point 2, this was operation was called Operation Pancir-2 and, again reference to Operation Pancir-2 at the very end of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 33007 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is a 9 February 1994 SRK command report from General Galic from the Butile forward command post to the VRS Main Staff, which says to the Lukavica KM for their information. If we could focus on item 5 of the report which is on page 2 in both versions, General Galic states, among other things: "The directives and decisions of the Supreme Command are being implemented." Then under item 8, General Galic states: "The decision on further operations remains unchanged. Active and decisive defence of all positions while creating conditions for the continuation of Operation Pancir and camouflaging of defensive positions in keeping with the new military and political situation." This Chamber has received evidence that there was quite significant activity, shelling activity that commenced at around the 20th of December 1993 coinciding with these operations and they continued throughout the month of January and in early February. Do you agree that this report here shows that the directives and supplements that were issued by General Mladic were continued to be in effect and the SRK was continuing with Operation Pancir between the end of December 1993 and 9 February 1994?

utterances.speaker: MITAR KOVAC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree in that particular way. This is a different interpretation of the actual situation on the ground. If you wish, I can explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Prosecution tenders the last document into evidence and I believe, yes, the Defence for an opportunity to potentially have a moment at the end of today's proceedings and I can stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will at least adjourn for the day very soon. Witness -- first of all -- no, we can deal with that once the witness has left the courtroom. Witness, we'd like to see you back at 9:30 in the morning on Tuesday, I think, it would be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I just -- could the parties assist me? The videolink evidence for Monday how much time would that take.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It's not videolink, it's live. It may take a part of Tuesday as well, based upon the estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please -- could you please remain available on Tuesday, the 24th of November in the morning hours, when, most likely, we'll resume hearing your testimony. And I again instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony. If that's clear, you may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the last document tendered, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 65 ter number 33007 receives exhibit number P7690.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P7690 is admitted into evidence. Mr. Lukic [sic], you have drawn our attention to paragraph 3. Mr. Ivetic, yes. I'm in a bad condition today. Mr. Ivetic, you have drawn our attention to paragraph 438 of the witness's report. Could you perhaps verify because I see that one of the sources there is again Radinovic expert report in 2000 with a page numbers on it and there are a few other footnotes there, where it's a bit unclear to me whether that's material which is in evidence or is not in evidence, such as a statement Mr. Koljevic apparently gave to the Defence, so that we have an opportunity to -- to further look into what you've drawn our attention to. Then the last matter Mr. Weber raised -- I leave that in the hands of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, you wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I do. Before we get to that, I believe Your Honour meant paragraph 4.39, not 4.38, since the citations you're reading are from that paragraph, which is the paragraph I cited to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. 4.39. That's what I had in my mind. Footnote 252 and the previous ones. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, first of all, my apologies to the Chamber if my perhaps inartful manner of trying to exercise my professional duties in compliance with my professional obligations caused you dismay. I stand by the fact that Judge Orie's question, neither read into the record the words and text of the paragraph he was citing which was 4.148, nor the preceding paragraph, 4.147 which I believe both parts contain precisely the language and facts which the Judge's question, as formulated, asserted that the witness had not written in his report. In such circumstances, I believe it is my obligation to correct the record. And that's all I have to say. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, I think it's not time to discuss it at length, but one thing I would like to draw your attention to, that is -- just a moment. Page 55, line 13, and -- no, 56, line 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE SAID
utterances.text: "You are clearly distinguishing between the responsibility of the authorities and the civilian population failure to comply with the safety measures by going out unnecessarily." Judge Orie made it very clear that there are -- that the report refers, on one the hand, to the authorities and, on the other hand, to the civilian population, that they failed to recognise their safety needs. I leave it to that. I take it that you apologised in a very reserved manner. I think we should leave it to that for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll adjourn for the day and resume on Monday, the 23rd of November, 9.30 in the morning, in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 23rd day of November, 2015, at 9.30 a.m.
